newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Wages data keeps economists guessing about rates.
newsitem.headline: Wages data keeps economists guessing about rates.

text.p: Long-awaited Australian wages data on Thursday proved more confusing than helpful to financial markets looking for clues as to whether there was room in the economy for another rate cut.
A strong rise in private sector earnings contrasted with a downward revision to previous data which had suggested some quickening in the overall pace of wages.

Average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 1.0 percent in the three months to February, leading to annual growth of 4.3 percent. This was a downward revision on preliminary data released earlier this month showing a 1.3 percent quarterly rise and a 4.6 percent annual rate.
While that downward revision was seen as a positive for the wages outlook, the split between private and public sector wages contained in the data caused some concern.
Private sector AWOTE by 1.3 percent in the quarter, to be 3.6 percent higher over the year. Public sector AWOTE rose 0.7 percent in the quarter, leaving it up 7.1 percent over the year.
"The overall revision down is a good result, but offsetting that is the private sector growth of 1.3 percent for the quarter," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Tony Meer said.
With some data showing a quickening and others a slowing in wages growth, economists' opinions on what it did to the interest rate outlook were mixed.

Some felt the fact total AWOTE remained near 4.5 percent, the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) "line in the sand" on wages growth, and the strong quarterly private sector AWOTE meant a rate cut was unlikely, with rates staying on hold at 6.00 percent for some time or rising at the end of this year.
The head of the Australian Treasury, Ted Evans, did not appear to be too concerned about signs of rising wages when asked about the data at a business economists lunch in Sydney.

"The best one could draw out of those figures is that we've been running at one percent a quarter for some time,...so it's doubtful that's there's been an acceleration as such," he said, but added that was still high for a low inflation environment.
The RBA has said that an acceleration in wages posed the greatest threat to its aim of maintaining the underlying rate of inflation to between two and three percent over a run of years.

"Wages growth remains too close to the boundary of being a potential threat to the Reserve Bank's two to three percent target to permit another cash rate cut," UBS Australian chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
Others, however, felt the downwards revision to overall AWOTE, and the fact the private sector AWOTE remained well under 4.5 percent suggested there was still room for a cut.
"The figures aren't as bad as they first look," Prudential Bache chief economist Dennis Mahoney said.
"The fact that private sector wages are only growing around 3.5 percent suggests the Reserve Bank really doesn't need to worry," he said.
Public sector AWOTE was largely discounted by economists as it has been distorted by government cutbacks and so is not considered accurate by policy makers or the market.
As well, private sector wages are seen as a better indicator of the inflation pressures flowing from wages rises.

"There's a bit of everything in the data, but in net terms I'd say it still suggests that the outlook for inflation is still pretty good," ANZ Treasury senior economist David de Garis said, adding he felt overall the data probably added slightly to the easing case.
